title: The ENTIRE History of Spain in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Spain in 10 Minutes (Romans to Democracy)
description:
From Phoenician traders and Roman Hispania to al-Andalus, El Cid, the fall of Granada, the empire of Charles V, Napoleon's invasion, the Disaster of 1898, the Civil War, Franco and the return of democracy: this is the whole story of Spain in about ten minutes. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #spain #spanishhistory #reconquista #animatedhistory

beats.say: January 2, 1492. The last Muslim king in Spain rides out of his palace to hand over the keys.

tag.text: Muhammad XII, last king of Granada

beats.say: Waiting for him are Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand, the rulers of Castile and Aragon.
That handover ended almost eight centuries of Muslim kingdoms in Spain.
And seven months later, the same queen sent a sailor named Columbus west, across the ocean.
Within a century, Spain ruled one of the biggest empires in history.
So how did one corner of Europe get there, lose it all, and end up a democracy? Let's start at the very beginning.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Spain in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From Romans to Reconquista to democracy

beats.say: First, the map. Spain shares a big square of land with Portugal, called the Iberian Peninsula.
Long ago, it was home to peoples like the Iberians and the Celts, living in fortified hill towns.
Sailors and traders from the east, the Phoenicians, built a port at Cádiz nearly three thousand years ago. It's one of the oldest cities in Western Europe.
Then, in 218 BC, Rome showed up to fight its great enemy, Carthage. And Rome stayed for about six hundred years.
Conquering the whole peninsula took the Romans about two hundred years. They called it Hispania. That's where the name Spain comes from.
They built roads, cities and aqueducts. The one in Segovia still stands, held up without any mortar.
Spain even gave Rome some of its best emperors. Trajan was born in Italica, near Seville, and the family of the next emperor, Hadrian, came from there too.
When Rome's empire fell apart in the 400s, a Germanic people called the Visigoths took over. They made Toledo their capital.
The Visigoth kings had one big weakness. They kept fighting each other for the throne.
I am the rightful king!
No, I am! Get off my chair!
In 711, while they argued, an army of Arabs and Berbers from North Africa crossed the narrow sea into Spain.
Its commander was Tariq ibn Ziyad. A big rock near where they landed is still named after him: Jabal Tariq, the Mountain of Tariq. Today we say Gibraltar.
The Visigoth king was defeated. Within a few years, almost all of the peninsula was under Muslim rule. They called it al-Andalus.
Its capital, Córdoba, became one of the biggest and richest cities in Europe, with paved streets, libraries and a giant mosque.

tag.text: Abd al-Rahman III, caliph of Córdoba

beats.say: In 929, its ruler, Abd al-Rahman the Third, even declared himself caliph, a title claiming leadership of the whole Muslim world.
Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side. Not always peacefully, but scholars, doctors and poets did great work.
Farmers in al-Andalus also spread new crops, like rice, sugar cane and oranges.
But in the mountains of the far north, a small Christian kingdom held on.
Tradition says it started at Covadonga, around 722, where a nobleman named Pelayo beat a Muslim force. Historians argue about how big that battle really was.
Over the centuries, Christian kingdoms like Castile and Aragon pushed south. Spaniards call it the Reconquista, the reconquest.
Its most famous warrior was Rodrigo Díaz, nicknamed El Cid, from the Arabic word for lord.
Plot twist: he fought for Christian and Muslim rulers, depending on who he was working for. In 1094, he took Valencia and ruled it himself.
A famous legend says that after he died, his men tied his body onto his horse to scare the enemy. Fun story, but it's a legend.
Spain's oldest great poem tells his story. Watching him ride by, the crowd cries: God, what a good vassal, if only he had a good lord!

show.text: God, what a good vassal, if only he had a good lord!
show.who: Cantar de mio Cid, Spain's epic poem, about 1200

beats.say: In 1469, Isabella of Castile married Ferdinand of Aragon, the heir to its throne.
Castile is mine.
And Aragon is mine.
So most of Spain is ours. Nice.
In January 1492, they took Granada, the last Muslim kingdom. About seven hundred and eighty-one years after 711, the Reconquista was over.

show.label: From 711 to 1492
show.sub: from the Muslim conquest to the fall of Granada

beats.say: That year also had a dark side. Spain ordered its Jews to convert or leave, and tens of thousands lost their homes. Muslims were later forced to choose too.
And in August, Columbus sailed west for Isabella and reached the Americas. The world was about to change.
Two years later, Spain and Portugal split the new lands with a line down the map, in the Treaty of Tordesillas.
Isabella and Ferdinand's grandson, Charles, won the biggest inheritance jackpot in history.
Your Majesty, you've inherited Spain, and its lands in the Americas!
Also the Netherlands, southern Italy, and Austria!
Is there anything I don't own?
In 1519, he was also elected Holy Roman Emperor, ruler of much of Germany. People said the sun never set on his lands.
Meanwhile, Spanish conquistadors seized huge empires in the Americas, often brutally. European diseases killed millions of Native people.
His son, Philip the Second, ran that empire from a giant palace and monastery called El Escorial.
He even got a country named after him: the Philippines.
This was Spain's Golden Age, with famous painters like El Greco and Velázquez.
But ruling half the world meant wars on every side: against France, the Ottomans, the Dutch and England.
Spain's royal family, the Habsburgs, kept marrying close relatives to hold on to power.
That likely caused real health problems. The last of them, Charles the Second, was sick his whole life, and had no children.

tag.text: Charles II, last Habsburg king of Spain

beats.say: People back then blamed witchcraft, so he was nicknamed the Bewitched. Doctors today point to the family marriages instead.
When he died in 1700, Europe fought a thirteen-year war over his throne: the War of the Spanish Succession.
The winner was a French prince, Philip of Bourbon, King Louis the Fourteenth's grandson. Spain's royal family today descends from him.
But the peace deal cost Spain. Britain took Gibraltar, the old Mountain of Tariq, and still has it today.
And in 1785, King Charles the Third picked a red and yellow flag for his navy, because it was easy to spot at sea. It's the base of Spain's flag today.
In 1808, Napoleon, the emperor of France, pressured Spain's royal family into giving up the throne.
Joseph, my brother, you are now the king of Spain.
Wonderful. Do the Spanish know that?
They'll get used to it.
They did not get used to it. On May 2, 1808, the people of Madrid rose up, and the revolt spread across the country.
Small bands ambushed French soldiers, then vanished into the hills. Spaniards called it a little war: guerrilla. That's where the word comes from.
Meanwhile, in the port of Cádiz, Spaniards wrote their first constitution, in 1812. Its supporters called themselves liberales, the first liberals in politics.
With British help, Spain and Portugal pushed the French out by 1814.
But with Spain in chaos, its colonies in the Americas broke away. By 1825, almost all of them were independent.
Spain kept Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines. Until 1898, when it lost a quick war with the United States.
Spain gave up almost all of its last colonies. Spaniards still call it, simply, the Disaster.

show.label: The war of 1898
show.sub: Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines

beats.say: In 1918, a deadly flu swept the world. Spain was neutral in World War One, so its newspapers reported it openly, while countries at war hid it. So it got called the Spanish flu, though it probably didn't start there.
In 1931, Spain's king left the country, and Spain became a republic.
But the country was badly divided, between left and right, and between rich and poor.
In 1936, army generals rebelled, and Spain fell into a terrible civil war. It lasted three years, and hundreds of thousands of people died.
General Francisco Franco won. He ruled as a dictator for thirty-six years, and opponents were jailed or worse.
From the 1960s, tourists poured onto Spain's beaches, and the economy boomed.
Franco died in 1975. The new king, Juan Carlos, helped steer Spain toward democracy. In 1978, Spaniards voted for a new constitution.
Then, in February 1981, armed police officers stormed parliament and held the lawmakers hostage, trying to bring back military rule.
In the middle of the night, the king went on TV and ordered the army to back democracy. By the next day, the coup had collapsed.
In 1986, Spain joined what is now the European Union. Today it's one of the most visited countries on Earth.
So that's Spain: Romans, Visigoths, caliphs, El Cid, an empire on which the sun never set, and finally, a democracy.
Next up: the weirdest Crusades in history. See you there.
